news.content: This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk . Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-reports-2026-to-2027-season/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-report-5-november-2026-week-45 This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. The report is based on data up to week 44 of 2026 (26 October to 1 November 2026). The main messages of this report are: Annual reports for the 2025 to 2026 season: Influenza in the UK, annual epidemiological report: winter 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Epidemiology of COVID-19 in England (published 25 June 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in all GP patients: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in school-aged children: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in frontline healthcare workers: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Influenza activity showed variable trends across surveillance indicators and is circulating at low levels. Emergency department ( ED ) attendances for influenza-like-illness ( ILI ) increased slightly and were above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection ( ARI ) incidents decreased compared with the previous week. A briefing note has been issued to inform the NHS that influenza activity is now above baseline levels. Influenza vaccination data was unavailable or incomplete at the time of analysis in weeks 41 and 42 and led to several cohorts not being published in week 42. This has been corrected since week 43, and all cohorts are included. This will be corrected retrospectively in the report for week 42. There remains an issue that affects the attribution of vaccinations by provider setting. The correct identification of vaccinations administered in pharmacies cannot currently be reliably distinguished from those administered in general practices or other healthcare settings. As a result, some pharmacy vaccinations are likely to be misclassified as general practice or other healthcare settings, artificially increasing vaccination activity reported for general practices and other healthcare settings and reducing activity reported for pharmacies. This is not expected to affect overall vaccination uptake estimates, which are considered to remain an accurate reflection of the influenza vaccination programme. Compared with the equivalent week last season (week 44 data, 2025 to 2026), vaccine uptake is lower among patients aged 65 years and over (59.1% vs 61.5%), patients aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups (27.9% vs 28.9%), those aged 2 years (33.3% vs 34.2%), and those aged 3 years (33.1% vs 34.3%). In contrast, vaccine uptake is higher among pregnant women (31.1% vs 29.7%). COVID-19 activity decreased and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness remained stable. The number of COVID-19 confirmed acute respiratory infections ( ARI ) incidents decreased compared with the previous week. By the end of week 44 2026, 47.7% of all people aged 75 years and over in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose. Similarly, 20.5% of all people aged under 75 years with a weakened immune system in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose since 1 October 2026. RSV activity increased and is circulating at baseline levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis increased and were within seasonally expected levels. Note 1: these indicators use the moving epidemic method ( MEM ) and the mean standard deviation method ( MSD ) to define thresholds to determine their respective levels of activity. Further information on these methods can be found in Influenza surveillance in Europe: establishing epidemic thresholds by the Moving Epidemic Method and Setting thresholds to determine COVID-19 activity levels using the mean standard deviation ( MSD ) method, England, 2022 to 2024 . The MEM approach is well-established for some influenza surveillance indicators, however, for other indicators both the MEM and MSD are experimental and may be subject to future revision. Influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using MEM to using MSD . These approaches will be considered alongside expert opinion and triangulation of other data sources. The Second Generation Surveillance System ( SGSS ) captures test result information for notifiable infectious diseases, including COVID-19 and influenza, from laboratories in England. The unified sample dataset ( USD ) stores all SARS-CoV-2 test results reported to SGSS , Respiratory DataMart and UKHSA laboratories, and is used to calculate the percentage of tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 among all SARS-CoV-2 tests conducted. As of 3 November 2026, there were a total of 1,730 COVID-19 cases identified in hospital settings in week 44, decreasing from 2,052 cases in the previous week. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) PCR positivity in hospital settings decreased slightly in week 44, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 7.6% up to Sunday 1 November 2026 compared with 8.1% for the same period on the previous Sunday. Positivity rates were highest among those aged 85 years and over with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 11.1% up to Sunday 1 November 2026. This has remained stable compared to 10.8% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Note 2: data from previous seasons is aligned by day. Note 3: testing policy and practice may change over time which can impact positivity rates, therefore comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution. Notable changes in testing policy occurred during 2022 to 2023, which are outlined in the data quality report . Note 4: the highlighted line corresponds to the age group in the subplot title, grey lines correspond to all other age groups. Influenza positivity increased in week 44, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 7.6% up to Sunday 1 November 2026. This is compared with 6.8% on the previous Sunday. By type, influenza A positivity increased in week 44, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 6.8% up to Sunday 1 November 2026. Influenza B positivity remained stable in the same week, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 0.3% up to Sunday 1 November 2026. Influenza A positivity rates were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 10.7% up to Sunday 1 November 2026. This has decreased from 15.8% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Influenza B positivity rates for the same period were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 1.0%. This has decreased from 2.0% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. RSV swab-positivity based PCR test results reported through SGSS have been included as a pilot indicator from week 49 2025 onwards. RSV positivity increased in week 44, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 2.5% up to Sunday 1 November 2026, compared with 1.6% up to the previous Sunday. RSV positivity rates were highest in those aged between 0 and 4 years with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 16.0% up to Sunday 1 November 2026 in week 44. This has increased from 10.0% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Respiratory DataMart is a sentinel laboratory-based surveillance system where participating laboratories report positive and negative test results for a number of respiratory viruses from samples primarily taken in hospital. A small proportion of primary care samples are also included in this reporting. In week 44, data is based on reporting from 9 out of the 14 sentinel laboratories. In week 44, 4,137 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for influenza. There were 307 positive samples for influenza: 221 influenza A (not subtyped), 7 influenza A (H3N2), 72 influenza A (H1N1)pdm09, and 11 influenza B. Overall, influenza positivity increased slightly to 7.4% in week 44 compared with 6.4% in the previous week. In week 44, 4,918 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for SARS-CoV-2. There were 367 positive samples for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable at 7.5% compared with 7.7% in the previous week, with the highest positivity in those aged 80 years and over at 9.9%. RSV positivity increased to 2.9%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 17.5%. Adenovirus positivity increased slightly to 1.6%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 8.4%. Human metapneumovirus ( hMPV ) positivity increased to 0.7%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 2.0%. Parainfluenza positivity increased to 3.6%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 13.5%. Rhinovirus positivity decreased slightly to 14.6%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 31.6%. DataMart data is provisional and subject to retrospective updates. Note 5: shading represents 95% confidence intervals. UKHSA conducts genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 lineages. This section provides an overview of circulating lineages in England, derived from data on sequenced PCR -positive SARS-CoV-2 samples in SGSS . The prevalence of UKHSA -designated lineages among sequenced cases is presented in Figure 13. To account for reporting delays, we report the proportion of lineages within COVID-19 cases that have had a sequenced positive sample between 28 September 2026 and 11 October 2026. Note that low sequencing numbers, especially within the latest reporting period, will impact the accuracy of the prevalence estimates. These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. The data quality report contains more information on lineage groupings. Analysis of viruses from primary and secondary care shows that circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses show low genetic diversity and all belong to clade D.3.1.1. Observations published from the WHO influenza vaccine composition meeting (VCM) in September 2026 suggest low reactivity of some viruses within the D.3.1.1 subclade with post-infection ferret antisera raised against A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus – the A(H1N1)pdm09 component in 2026 Southern and 2026/2027 Northern Hemisphere cell- and egg-based influenza vaccines - and human sera post-vaccination with the Southern Hemisphere vaccine 2026. It is not yet clear how vaccine effectiveness against clinical disease may be affected by these observations. Vaccines typically still provide protection against severe clinical disease when drifted strains are seen with only a modest reduction in effectiveness. The characterisation of circulating A(H3N2) viruses shows that A(H3N2) viruses are currently showing low genetic diversity. All sequenced viruses to date belong to genetic subclade K. To date, only a small number of influenza B viruses have been detected, which show some genetic diversity. Between week 35 2026 (week ending 30 August 2026) and week 44 2026 (week ending 1 November 2026), the UKHSA respiratory virus unit ( RVU ) has genetically characterised 351 seasonal influenza viruses, and identified 229 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, 90 influenza A(H3N2) viruses, and 32 influenza B viruses. Details of the characterised viruses by subtype are shown in Tables 1, 2 and 3. The RVU has confirmed by genome sequencing the detection of live attenuated influenza vaccine ( LAIV ) viruses in 14 influenza A/B positive samples, collected from children aged between 2 and 16 years. UKHSA RVU performs antigenic characterisation of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, influenza A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses using haemagglutination inhibition ( HI ) assays. Data from these assays are used to compare how similar the currently circulating influenza viruses are to the strains included in seasonal influenza vaccines, and to monitor for changes in circulating influenza viruses. Similarity of currently circulating influenza strains to vaccine strains is defined as having an antibody titre within 4-fold when compared with reference viruses representative of the vaccine strain. Antigenic characterisation of viruses in the current reporting period is underway. A(H1N1)pdm09: 5 A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses have been antigenically characterised and 3 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H1N1)pdm09 vaccine strains. A(H3N2): 6 A(H3N2) viruses have been antigenically characterised and 6 were similar to reference viruses representative of the A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like and A/Darwin/1415/2025 (H3N2)-like Northern Hemisphere 2026/27 (H3N2) vaccine strains. Influenza positive samples are screened for mutations in the virus neuraminidase ( NA ) and the cap-dependent endonuclease of the polymerase acidic protein (PA) genes known to confer neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir and zanamivir) or baloxavir resistance, respectively. Results from this surveillance are given in table 4. There have been six detections with mutations related to reduced susceptibility/resistance to oseltamivir and/or reduced susceptibility to baloxavir. Data is presented on viral ARI incidents in different settings that are reported to UKHSA health protection teams ( HPTs ). Please note that reporting practices are known to vary between seasons and between regions. Any interpretation of temporal and regional trends should consider the likelihood of differences in reporting of ARI incidents over time and between regions. There were 103 new ARI incidents reported in week 44 in England. These included: 95 incidents from care homes, of which 16 were due to influenza A, 12 were due to SARS-CoV-2, 11 were due to other pathogens, 4 were due to multiple pathogens and 1 was due to influenza (no type information available). No pathogen was reported in 51 incidents 1 incident from hospitals, of which 1 was due to multiple pathogens 3 incidents from educational settings, of which 3 were due to RSV 4 incidents from other settings, of which 2 were due to SARS-CoV-2. No pathogen was reported in 2 incidents Syndromic surveillance collects data from various healthcare sources where presentations are classified by patterns of symptoms compatible with specific infections. In some settings, the syndromic diagnosis can be supplemented by (rapid) testing. In this report, ED attendances are displayed. Further details and data from other syndromic surveillance systems can be found in the syndromic surveillance weekly summaries . During the week ending on 01 November 2026, ED attendances for acute respiratory infections remained stable overall, however there were increases in the under 1 year age group. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness remained stable. ED attendance for influenza-like illness increased slightly and were above seasonally expected levels; the increase was in adults aged 45 to 64 years. ED attendance for acute bronchiolitis (a syndrome related to RSV infection) increased and were within seasonally expected levels. Daily NHS 111 acute respiratory infection triaged calls remained stable. GP in-hours consultation rates for upper respiratory tract infections remained stable overall and at seasonally expected levels; however there were increases observed in the under 1 year age group. Consultations for bronchiolitis increased in the under 1 year age group while COVID-19-like and influenza-like illness consultations both decreased. GP out-of-hours daily contacts for acute respiratory infections were stable. Note 6: 7-day moving average is adjusted for bank holidays. Grey columns show weekends and bank holidays. Note 7: the coloured line is the 7-day moving average by age group. Grey lines show the other age groups. The y-axis shows daily attendances. It is adjusted for bank holidays. Primary care surveillance is undertaken in collaboration with the Royal College of General Practitioners ( RCGP ) Research and Surveillance Centre ( RSC ), using a national sentinel surveillance system of around 2,000 GP practices covering over 20 million registered patients of all ages across England. More information on the methodology can be found in the data quality report . The weekly ILI consultation rate through the RCGP surveillance decreased slightly to 6.2 per 100,000 registered population in participating GP practices in week 44 compared with 6.5 per 100,000 in the previous week. This rate is in the baseline activity level (Figure 20). By age group, the highest rates were seen in those aged under 1 year (12.0 per 100,000), and those aged between 1 and 4 years (8.8 per 100,000). The lower respiratory tract infections ( LRTI ) consultation rate remained stable at 84.1 per 100,000 in week 44 compared with 81.6 per 100,000 in the previous week. Further details are available in the weekly RSC communicable and respiratory disease report for England . MEM thresholds are based on data from the 2018 to 2019 season to the 2025 to 2026 season. Note the 2019 to 2020, 2020 to 2021 and 2021 to 2022 seasons have been removed. From wee…

These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. analysis.time: The report is based on data up to week 44 of 2026 (26 October to 1 November 2026) [N5]. The publication date is 5 November 2026 [N4].
analysis.location_and_population: The report covers England, focusing on influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and COVID-19 activity in the population [N4].
analysis.event: The report summarizes influenza activity, noting that it is circulating at low levels and that ED attendances for influenza-like-illness increased slightly above seasonally expected levels [N7]. It also mentions that influenza-confirmed ARI incidents decreased compared with the previous week [N8].
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Influenza activity showed variable trends across surveillance indicators, with ED attendances for ILI slightly above baseline and ARI incidents decreasing [N7, N8]. Vaccine uptake data indicated lower rates among certain age groups and clinical risk groups compared to the previous season [N17].
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: A briefing note was issued to inform the NHS about influenza activity being above baseline levels [N9]. There are noted issues with the correct identification of vaccinations administered in pharmacies versus general practices, which may affect the classification of vaccination activity [N15].

analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 5 November 2026 (week 45) provides an overview of influenza activity in England, based on data up to week 44 (26 October to 1 November 2026). It notes that influenza is circulating at low levels, with a slight increase in emergency department (ED) attendances for influenza-like-illness (ILI) above seasonally expected levels. Influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection (ARI) incidents decreased compared to the previous week. Vaccine uptake data shows lower rates among older adults and those in clinical risk groups compared to the previous season, while pregnant women had higher uptake. The report also mentions that there are ongoing challenges in accurately attributing vaccinations administered in pharmacies to the correct provider setting, which may affect reported activity levels. Additionally, it highlights that COVID-19 activity decreased, with ARI incidents also declining, and RSV activity increased but remained within baseline levels. The report serves as a summary of surveillance data for multiple respiratory viruses, including influenza, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2, and is intended to inform public health responses.

news.title: Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 dominant in Thailand, but remains responsive to treatment - Thai PBS World
news.rss_summary_html: Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 dominant in Thailand, but remains responsive to treatment  Thai PBS World
news.excerpt_original: Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 dominant in Thailand, but remains responsive to treatment Thai PBS World

news.content: Skip to main content Accessibility Text Size A−AA+A++ Line Spacing NormalMoreMost Color Blind Mode OffProtanDeutanTritan Dark Mode Toggle Dark Mode High Contrast Toggle High Contrast Grayscale Toggle Grayscale Readable Font Toggle Readable Font Highlight Links Toggle Highlight Links Focus Highlight Toggle Focus Highlight Hide Images Toggle Hide Images Reduce Motion Toggle Reduce Motion Home News Around Thailand Politics Economy ASEAN Environment Lifestyles World Analysis Opinion ProgrammesGalleryInfographicQuotesAbout Us Login One Member Home News Programmes Gallery Infographic Quotes About Us Search Health Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 dominant in Thailand, but remains responsive to treatment 06 Nov 2026 ThaiPBS AI In Brief Share The Department of Medical Sciences has confirmed that Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 was the most dominant flu strain detected in Thailand between January and October this year, reassuring the public that genomic monitoring showed no signs of antiviral drug resistance. Dr. Adisorn Wathanasak, director-general of the Department of Medical Sciences, stated that surveillance data gathered by the Thai National Influenza Center, a World Health Organization (WHO) regional reference laboratory, analysed 8,734 patient samples during the ten-month period. Out of the total samples collected, 1,278 tested positive for influenza, representing a positivity rate of 14.63%. Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 accounted for the majority of detections, comprising 704 cases or 55.09% of all positive samples. This was followed by Influenza A(H3N2) with 306 cases (23.94%) and Influenza B of the Victoria lineage with 268 cases (20.97%). The dominance of A(H1N1)pdm09 surged even further in October, where it represented 115 out of 122 positive cases, or 94.26%, from 581 patient samples submitted during the month. In contrast, Influenza A(H3N2) dropped to 2.46% (3 cases) and Influenza B accounted for 3.28% (4 cases). Detailed genetic sequencing showed that the A(H1N1)pdm09 clade 6B.1A.5a.2a.1 has increased significantly since June and remains the primary circulating subtype. Meanwhile, the K clade was identified as the main variant for Influenza A(H3N2) throughout the surveillance period, while the V1A.3a.2 clade was the main variant detected for Influenza B. Regarding drug resistance monitoring, laboratory analysis of the Neuraminidase (NA) gene across tested specimens, including 127 samples analyzed specifically in October, showed no evidence of mutations that indicate resistance to antiviral therapies. Crucially, tests confirmed the absence of the H275Y mutation in A(H1N1)pdm09, which is linked to Oseltamivir resistance. No other genetic mutations associated with reduced sensitivity to neuraminidase inhibitors were found across any of the circulating strains. Dr. Adisorn emphasised that ongoing surveillance of viral clades, genetic alterations, and drug resistance remains essential for evaluating transmission trends and supporting public health interventions. He advised members of the public to maintain good personal hygiene and follow public health guidelines to reduce the risk of infection and prevent the spread of the virus. analysis.brief_en: In Thailand, Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 has been confirmed as the dominant flu strain from January to October 2026, according to the Department of Medical Sciences. Surveillance data from the Thai National Influenza Center, a WHO regional reference laboratory, showed that 1,278 out of 8,734 patient samples tested positive for influenza, with A(H1N1)pdm09 accounting for 55.09% of these cases. In October alone, A(H1N1)pdm09 represented 94.26% of positive cases from 581 samples. Detailed genetic sequencing revealed the A(H1N1)pdm09 clade 6B.1A.5a.2a.1 as the primary circulating subtype. Laboratory analysis confirmed no evidence of antiviral drug resistance, including the absence of the H275Y mutation linked to Oseltamivir resistance. Public health officials emphasized the importance of continued monitoring and adherence to hygiene guidelines to manage the outbreak effectively.

news.content_zh: 根据泰国医学科学部的报告,2026年1月至10月期间,流感甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09在泰国被确认为占主导地位的流感毒株。泰国国家流感中心(WHO区域参考实验室)提供的监测数据显示,8734份患者样本中有1278份检测出流感病毒,其中甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09占55.09%。仅在10月,581份样本中有94.26%为甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09阳性。详细基因测序显示,甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09的6B.1A.5a.2a.1分支是主要流行的亚型。实验室分析确认未发现与奥司他韦耐药性相关的H275Y 突变耐药性证据。公共卫生官员强调,持续监测病毒分支、基因变异和耐药性对于有效管理暴发至关重要。

news.content: The number of children hospitalized with seasonal flu is increasing, raising concerns about the risk of complications. Seasonal influenza spreads rapidly and can cause complications in young children, requiring parents to pay close attention to monitoring and prevention. Báo Hải Phòng • 04/11/2026 The patient came for examination at Hai Duong Pediatric Hospital. According to Hai Duong Pediatric Hospital, in the past five weeks, the hospital has received and treated 320 cases of seasonal influenza, a significant increase compared to previous periods. Seasonal influenza is a respiratory infectious disease caused by the influenza virus, with influenza A and influenza B viruses being the most common causative agents. Most children with the flu recover after a period of time. However, the disease still carries the risk of becoming severe and causing complications, especially in children under 5 years old, premature babies, underweight children, malnourished children, children with chronic diseases, or those with weakened immune systems. You may also like Proactively protect children from seasonal flu with needle-free nasal spray vaccines. GD&TĐ - Given the complex developments of the flu epidemic, experts advise parents to proactively take early preventive measures for their children to prevent dangerous complications. Seasonal influenza can cause serious complications in children; parents should proactively take preventive measures. Seasonal influenza can cause serious complications, even death, in otherwise healthy children. Doctors advise parents to recognize early signs of worsening symptoms and proactively take annual flu preventative measures for their children. Signs and symptoms that may indicate you have the flu. Seasonal influenza has shown a slight increase in recent weeks. Children with the disease may experience a sudden high fever, cough, runny nose, and body aches. Common symptoms of the flu in children include sudden fever, chills, cough, sore throat, runny nose, headache, body aches, and fatigue. Some children may experience stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. In young children, symptoms are sometimes subtle, mainly manifesting as fussiness, poor feeding, reduced appetite, or less activity than usual. Notably, influenza can progress severely with symptoms such as rapid breathing, difficulty breathing, chest retraction, bluish lips, lethargy, difficulty waking up, seizures, refusal to feed, inability to drink, or signs of dehydration. If a child's fever and cough have subsided but then return, and their health deteriorates, parents should take the child to a medical facility immediately for examination and timely treatment. To prevent the disease, doctors advise parents to practice good personal hygiene, wash hands frequently with soap, cover their mouths when coughing or sneezing, keep the living environment well-ventilated, and limit children's contact with people who have symptoms of illness. If a child shows suspected flu symptoms, parents should take them to see a doctor and not self-medicate or treat them at home without guidance from a healthcare professional. You may also like Annual seasonal flu vaccination is an important measure to reduce the risk of illness and limit complications. Because the flu virus constantly mutates, immunity after vaccination can weaken over time, so children need booster shots as recommended. The hospital emphasizes the importance of early intervention and annual flu vaccinations to reduce the risk of complications. supplementary_news.content: Tr Tr Pamukkale University PAU Hospitals Issue a Warning: Let Us Take Precautions Against Seasonal Flu 04.11.2026 TR Assoc. Prof. Dr. Suna Seçil Öztürk Deniz, a faculty member of the Department of Infectious Diseases at Pamukkale University (PAU) Hospitals, made a statement about seasonal flu. In her statement, Assoc. Prof. Dr. Suna Seçil Öztürk Deniz, a faculty member of the Department of Infectious Diseases at PAU Hospitals, said: “With colder weather, an increase is being observed in upper respiratory tract infections and seasonal influenza cases. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Health recommend annual flu vaccination for high-risk groups, particularly healthcare professionals, as well as people with underlying health conditions, pregnant women, young children and older adults. Vaccination helps protect against influenza, reduce its spread and prevent the development of serious complications that can be life-threatening, particularly in high-risk groups. Seasonal influenza is an acute infection caused by influenza A and B viruses and can be transmitted through the respiratory route. Common symptoms include sudden onset of fever, cough, sore throat, headache, muscle and joint pain, and pronounced fatigue. Although most people recover from the illness within approximately one week, it can be severe in older adults, young children, pregnant women, people with chronic illnesses and those with weakened immune systems. When flu symptoms appear, it is important to rest, drink sufficient fluids and seek support from healthcare professionals when necessary. People in high-risk groups and those experiencing severe symptoms should seek medical attention without delay. Anyone experiencing shortness of breath, chest pain, changes in consciousness or a significant deterioration in their general condition should seek urgent medical assistance. Antiviral treatment may be administered to patients when deemed necessary by a physician; it is important to start this treatment early. Antibiotics are not effective against viruses and are not routinely used to treat influenza. Medications should be used in accordance with a physician’s advice.” “What should we pay attention to in order to protect ourselves against the flu?” Emphasising the importance of people in high-risk groups receiving the seasonal flu vaccine every year in accordance with their physicians’ recommendations, Assoc. Prof. Dr. Suna Seçil Öztürk Deniz continued: “Vaccination of healthcare professionals also helps protect both themselves and the people they care for. Wash your hands regularly with soap and water, and use an appropriate hand sanitiser when necessary. Cover your mouth and nose with a disposable tissue when coughing or sneezing; if no tissue is available, use the inside of your elbow. Avoid spending long periods in crowded and poorly ventilated places, and ventilate crowded indoor spaces frequently. Stay at home as much as possible. When you need to be in the same environment as others, wear a mask and reduce close contact. Get enough sleep, eat a balanced diet and drink sufficient fluids. To protect public and patient health and ensure patient safety, we invite all citizens and healthcare professionals to act responsibly and raise awareness about seasonal influenza, pay attention to hand hygiene as one of the basic methods of protection, follow respiratory hygiene rules such as wearing masks and maintaining physical distance, and receive the recommended vaccinations.” İlgili Haberler Sağlık Statement from PAU Hospitals on World Radiology Day, November 8: Radiology Is Where Scientific Knowledge Touches Human Lives 08.11.2026 Bilimsel “Orange” Solidarity at PAU DSBMYO: LÖSEV Awareness Day Gathering Held 05.11.2026 Sağlık PAU Hospitals Call for Organ Donation: The Greatest Legacy Is One Left for Future Generations, Not the Grave 03.11.2026 Sağlık PAU Hospitals Conduct Training Sessions to Raise Breast Cancer Awareness Across the University 02.11.2026 Sağlık PAU Hospitals Warn: Psoriasis Can Affect Not Only the Skin but Also the Joints 02.11.2026 Sağlık First Procedure Performed Using New Equipment at the PAU Hospitals Stroke Center 23.10.2026 Son Haberler Bu Hafta PAU WEEKLY AGENDA 20 Saat Önce Bilimsel PAU Academicians Conduct Inspections as Part of the RISE Türkiye Project 06.11.2026 Bilimsel “Orange” Solidarity at PAU DSBMYO: LÖSEV Awareness Day Gathering Held 05.11.2026 Bilimsel Scientific Studies by PAU Academician Featured in the University of Murcia Bulletin 05.11.2026 Uluslararası İlişkiler Provincial Directorate of Migration Management’s Mobile Migration Advisory Vehicle Begins Operations at PAU 03.11.2026

supplementary_news.content: 11°C broken clouds TFL Updates Search for: Search Search LDN Write For Us Login London News Lifestyle Entrepreneurship Fitness & Health Finance Tech Food & Drink Automotive Travel Global Canada approves first mRNA seasonal flu vaccine for over-50s By LDN Editor 06 November 2026 3 minute read Listen to this article Canada has become the first country to authorise an mRNA vaccine against seasonal influenza for adults aged 50 and over, approving Moderna’s mFLUSIVA for the 2026-27 respiratory season. The regulator also authorised mCOFLU, a combined mRNA vaccine against influenza and COVID-19, for the same age group. The decision was announced on 5 November after markets closed. What has been approved Health Canada’s authorisation covers adults aged 50 and above, a group that carries a disproportionate share of influenza hospitalisations and deaths. The approval follows the US Food and Drug Administration’s decision in August to authorise mFLUSIVA for the same age group. Seasonal flu vaccines have been made using chicken eggs or cultured cells for decades. The mRNA platform instead delivers genetic instructions that prompt the body to produce a viral protein, which the immune system then learns to recognise. The advantage claimed for the technology is speed. A conventional vaccine requires a strain to be grown and characterised months in advance, which is why the annual flu vaccine is sometimes a poor match for the virus that circulates. An mRNA vaccine can be updated to a new strain sequence in weeks rather than months. The regulatory bar Approval for a new flu vaccine platform requires evidence of immunogenicity, the ability to provoke an immune response, and of safety in a large population. It also requires evidence that the vaccine protects against strains that are circulating, which is harder to demonstrate when the virus changes each year. Regulators in several countries have been cautious about mRNA flu vaccines because the correlates of protection for influenza are less well established than for COVID-19. An authorisation for adults over 50 is a narrower approval than a universal one, and it will be followed by monitoring of real-world effectiveness during the season. The combined influenza and COVID-19 vaccine is the more commercially significant product, since it would reduce the number of injections in an annual campaign. Combination vaccines have historically been difficult to develop because the immune response to one component can interfere with the other. What it means for patients For most people over 50, the existing egg-based and cell-based vaccines remain effective and widely available. The mRNA products offer an alternative, not a replacement, and their uptake will depend on how they are priced and whether health systems recommend them. The timing of the authorisation means the vaccines are unlikely to be widely used in the current season, since procurement and distribution for the northern hemisphere campaign are largely settled by early autumn. The more realistic impact is in 2027-28 and beyond. Moderna has been under financial pressure as demand for its COVID-19 vaccine has fallen, and it has been cutting costs while trying to establish its respiratory vaccine portfolio. A first-in-world approval for an mRNA flu vaccine gives it a regulatory precedent it can use in other markets. The wider significance Influenza kills hundreds of thousands of people worldwide each year, and vaccine effectiveness varies widely depending on how well the chosen strains match those that circulate. A platform that can be updated quickly and manufactured at scale would reduce that variability. The approval also marks a shift in how regulators treat mRNA technology. What began as an emergency authorisation during a pandemic is now being assessed through the ordinary licensing pathway for a routine seasonal vaccine, which is a test of whether the platform can compete on cost and convenience with established manufacturers. Is a Mutated H1N1 Strain to Blame? Flu activity is surging earlier than usual as an influenza A H1N1 strain with a new mutation spreads across the U.S. Here’s what to know. Updated Nov. 6, 2026, 5:57 PM UTC / Source: TODAY Caroline Kee Health reporter 0 seconds of 3 minutes, 19 secondsVolume 0% Press shift question mark to access a list of keyboard shortcuts Keyboard ShortcutsEnabledDisabled Play/PauseSPACE Increase Volume↑ Decrease Volume↓ Seek Forward→ Seek Backward← Captions On/Offc Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreenf Mute/Unmutem Decrease Caption Size- Increase Caption Size+ or = Seek %0-9 Settings OffCCEnglish Font Color White Font Opacity 100% Font Size 100% Font Family Arial Character Edge None Background Color Black Background Opacity 50% Window Color Black Window Opacity 0% Reset WhiteBlackRedGreenBlueYellowMagentaCyan 100%75%50%25% 200%175%150%125%100%75%50% ArialCourierGeorgiaImpactLucida ConsoleTahomaTimes New RomanTrebuchet MSVerdana NoneRaisedDepressedUniformDrop Shadow WhiteBlackRedGreenBlueYellowMagentaCyan 100%75%50%25%0% WhiteBlackRedGreenBlueYellowMagentaCyan 100%75%50%25%0% Auto540p (1690 kbps)1080p (4670 kbps)720p (3360 kbps)540p (1690 kbps)360p (912 kbps)270p (486 kbps)270p (276 kbps) Live 00:02 03:17 03:19 Flu Season Kicks off Early: Is it Too Late to Get the Vaccine? 03:20 Share Savewith a NBCUniversal Profile Add TODAY to Google If you’re surprised to hear about people getting the flu in October, you’re not alone. The 2026-2027 flu season got off to an early and strong start in the United States, experts say. Influenza activity is still considered low nationally, but cases are rising quickly in many parts of the country, especially in the West. As of Nov. 5, flu infections are growing or likely growing in 42 states, according to the latest estimates from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That’s not unusual, given that flu activity typically ramps up around this time of year. However, this year’s flu season started way ahead of schedule, with infections rising as early as August. “Early-season influenza activity is currently higher than typically observed at this time of year,” the CDC said in its FluView surveillance report for the week ending Oct. 31. So far this season, there have been at least 1,700,000 illnesses, 25,000 hospitalizations and 1,400 deaths from the flu in the U.S., per the CDC. H1N1, a type of influenza A virus, is currently fueling the vast majority of cases. That’s a shift from last winter, when influenza A H3N2 subclade K (aka, the “superflu”) was the dominant strain nationwide. What’s more, it appears that the H1N1 strain circulating in the U.S. has picked up a new mutation which may affect its ability to evade pre-existing immunity, experts say. If H1N1 sounds familiar, that’s because it’s the infamous “swine flu” virus that caused a pandemic in 2009. As the mutated H1N1 strain spreads, doctors are urging people to get the 2026-2027 flu vaccine. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu season and how to protect yourself. Why Is Flu Season Starting So Early? No two flu seasons look the same because the timing and severity can vary from year to year. It’s still too early to tell if this flu season will end up being more severe or what role the mutated H1N1 strain might play, the CDC tells TODAY.com in a statement. However, there are multiple indicators that flu activity is already higher than usual for this time of year. Cases started increasing in late August and early September and have been rising steadily since, per the CDC. The percent of flu tests coming back positive was 9.1% during the week ending Oct. 31. Last year during the same time period, the weekly test positivity rate was less than 1%, per the CDC National Respiratory and Enteric Virus Surveillance System dashboard. Outpatient visits to healthcare providers for flu-like illness hit 2.8% during the week ending Oct. 17, which is higher than the previous two seasons, CDC data show. Hospitalizations and deaths from the flu are also rising. “Cases are still relatively low, so we’re still in the early phases of a flu surge,” Andrew Pekosz, Ph.D., a virologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. As of Oct. 31, seven states are reporting moderate to high levels of flu activity: California, Florida, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Texas and Washington. It’s unclear why exactly cases are rising earlier than normal. One potential reason is that people may have less pre-existing immunity to the H1N1 strain with a new mutation. “Maybe that’s why people are getting sick sooner,” Dr. Bernard Camins, an infectious disease physician and professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, tells TODAY.com. The H1N1 strain spreading is different from the H3N2 strain that dominated last winter. “Even people who got the flu last year are vulnerable,” says Camins. When H1N1 started ramping up in late August, the updated flu shots had just started rolling out. “The pattern we oftentimes see with early season flu is that the first strain that gets here is the one that escapes immunity the most,” Pekosz adds. Does an early flu season mean a more severe flu season? Not necessarily, experts say. “An earlier increase in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak,” the CDC said in its latest FluView report. It’s too early to tell how the 2026-2027 flu season will pan out, or whether it’ll be milder compared to last year’s season. The U.S. saw a harsh flu season last winter fueled by the highly mutated H3N2 subclade K variant, aka the “super flu.” “We still have to see how bad it will be this year, but I think it is just starting earlier,” says Camins. “The only thing predictable about the flu is that it’s unpredictable,” Dr. Natalie Azar, NBC News medical contributor, said on TODAY. What Is the Mutated H1N1 Strain? Influenza viruses mutate constantly, which is why we get an updated flu shot every year. Recommended Deals DealsDon’t Sleep on These Fall Finds From Lululemon’s ‘We Made Too Much’ Section Home HomeNeed Better Sleep? Experts Say Ergonomic Pillows Are the Answer for Better Support Last summer, flu A H3N2 picked up a host of mutations, which led to the emergence the subclade K variant. H1N1 viruses typically change less often than H3N2 viruses, the CDC says. However, this year, H1N1 (pdm09), subclade D.3.1.1, acquired one new mutation, G155E, says Pekosz. The mutation was first identified in September in Seattle, Washington, according in a preprint paper published to bioRxiv. “It is different from last year’s H1N1 virus, and that mutation position (G155E) we know is important for generating protective antibody responses,” Pekosz explains. This means the latest H1N1 strain may be better able to escape immunity because the antibodies people have from previous infection or vaccination may not recognize it as well. “How that (mutation) is going to affect the disease spread and severity is not clear,” says Pekosz. Even if the H1N1 strain circulating does not match the one included in the 2026-2027 flu vaccines, the shot is still expected to provide protection. “A mismatch is not a black-or-white situation. We may have less immunity, not no immunity,” Pekosz adds. Historically, H1N1 has hit young people particularly hard. The new mutation may make children more susceptible, especially if they haven’t been exposed to H1N1 yet, Azar said. “It is too early to know what viruses may predominate or to say whether there might be implications on flu vaccine effectiveness this season,” the CDC said in its latest FluView report. H1N1 Flu Symptoms Influenza often hits suddenly and intensely, says Camins. Common symptoms of the flu include: Fever Chills Fatigue Body aches Runny nose Coughing It can be difficult to distinguish the signs of a flu infection from those caused by COVID-19, which is why testing is important, Camins says. If you test positive for influenza, you can seek treatment with antivirals, which can lessen symptom severity and duration. Antivirals are an especially important tool for high-risk groups, including people over the age of 65, children under the age of 5, and immunocompromised individuals. These medications aren’t available over-the-counter, so you’ll need to see a doctor first. “You have to get that prescription fast ... within the first 48 hours after symptom onset, (or else) they don’t work as well,” says Pekosz. If you experience severe flu symptoms, contact your doctor. When to Get the Flu Shot There’s no reason to panic over the mutated H1N1 strain, the experts emphasize, but it is a good reminder to protect yourself. “View (this) as a a sign to go out and get the flu vaccine,” says Pekosz. Getting a flu shot is the most effective way to prevent against severe illness, complications and death from the flu. The 2026-2027 flu vaccines are available at most pharmacies, doctors’ offices and clinics. The updated shots protect against three viruses: influenza A H1N1 (pdm09), influenza A H3N2 and influenza B. There are multiple options available, including standard flu shots, high-dose shots, a nasal mist and the new mRNA flu vaccine. “Even if there’s a mismatched strain, there’s two other strains that the vaccine will provide better protection against,” says Pekosz. Different flu strains can circulate later in the season, so the shot can protect you throughout the winter and early spring. The flu shot is never 100% effective, Camins adds, and you can still get infected if you’ve been vaccinated — but you won’t get nearly as sick or end up in the hospital. Vaccination is especially important if you’re considered high-risk, but everyone can benefit. The best time to get the flu shot is before the end of October, but the vaccine will still provide protection if you get it later in the season, the experts note. “If you haven’t gotten it yet for whatever reason, now’s the time to get vaccinated because the flu season is starting a little bit sooner and you need at least two weeks for the vaccine immunity to (reach) protective levels,” Pekosz adds. If you aren’t sure which flu vaccine you should get, talk to your doctor or pharmacist. supplementary_news.content: メインコンテンツへスキップ What is the difference between Influenza A and B? | Explaining symptoms, testing, and vaccines 検査室からみる遺伝子と医療|臨床検査・研究・AI Nov 6, 2026 08:10 You were told you tested positive for Influenza A. Or perhaps you have heard a family member say they had Type B. Why is influenza divided into Type A and Type B, even though it is the same illness? Are the symptoms of Type A more severe? Is it true that Type B is less likely to cause a fever? Can you catch Type B after having Type A? I think some people have these questions. In fact, Type A and Type B are different classifications of the virus. However, you cannot determine whether it is Type A or Type B based on symptoms alone. In this article, from the perspective of a clinical laboratory technician working in a university hospital laboratory, I will explain the differences between Influenza A and B, what can be learned from testing, and the relationship with vaccines. Table of Contents 1. Are there types of influenza other than A and B? 2. What is the difference between Type A and Type B? Type A is classified by combinations of "H" and "N" Type B is classified by 'lineage' 3. Is type A more severe? Is type B milder? 4. How are type A and type B distinguished in tests? Even if it is type A positive, it is usually not known whether it is H1N1 or H3N2 Is there a difference in detection sensitivity between A and B? 5. Can I catch type B after having type A? 6. Does the vaccine cover both type A and type B? すべて表示 1. Are there types of influenza other than A and B? Influenza viruses are broadly classified into four types: A, B, C, and D. Among these, it is mainly Type A and Type B that cause the seasonal influenza that spreads almost every year. Type C also infects humans, but it generally only causes mild symptoms and does not cause major seasonal epidemics like Type A or B. Type D is a virus primarily related to animals such as cattle and has not been established as a cause of human influenza disease. When you take a rapid influenza test at a medical institution due to a fever or other symptoms, the reason you get a result of "Type A" or "Type B" is that general tests mainly target these two types. 2. What is the difference between Type A and Type B? Even though they are both influenza viruses, Type A and Type B have different classification mechanisms. Type A is classified by combinations of "H" and "N" Both Influenza A and B have proteins called hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) on their surfaces. HA is involved in the process of the virus binding to cells, and NA is involved in the process of the replicated virus being released from cells. Type A is further classified into "subtypes" based on the types of these proteins. For example, the following names are often heard. A (H1N1) subtype A (H3N2) subtype H1N1 indicates a combination of H1 for HA and N1 for NA. H3N2 follows the same logic. Currently, the main type A viruses circulating seasonally in humans are A (H1N1) pdm09 and A (H3N2). Additionally, type A viruses can infect not only humans but also various animals, such as birds and pigs. If a type A virus with new properties emerges and begins to spread efficiently from person to person, it could lead to a global pandemic. Type B is classified by 'lineage' On the other hand, while type B also has HA and NA, it is not classified into subtypes like H1N1 or H3N2 as type A is. For type B, the following two lineages are primarily known: Victoria lineage Yamagata lineage Of these, regarding the Yamagata lineage, no confirmed detections of naturally circulating viruses have been reported since March 2020. However, it has not been proven that it has completely disappeared. In recent years, the type B virus confirmed to be circulating in humans is the Victoria lineage. 3. Is type A more severe? Is type B milder? 'Type A causes high fever, but type B is relatively mild.' You may have heard something like that. However, it is not the case that type A always leads to severe illness or that type B always results in a mild case. Both type A and type B can cause fever, headache, muscle pain, joint pain, severe fatigue, cough, and sore throat. Also, influenza does not always cause a high fever. In some cases, such as in the elderly, it may not be accompanied by a typical high fever. In children, gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea may be seen, but it is not possible to determine that it is type B based on these symptoms alone. Furthermore, complications such as pneumonia or severe illness can occur with both type A and type B. Type B is sometimes thought of as a mild illness, but this is not necessarily the case. In other words, it is not possible to distinguish between type A and type B based solely on the severity of symptoms or the height of the fever. The possibility of severe illness must be judged by considering not only the virus type but also age, underlying medical conditions, and immune status. 4. How are type A and type B distinguished in tests? From here on, I will explain from the perspective of a laboratory. The rapid influenza antigen tests widely used in medical institutions detect specific proteins of the virus. In general rapid antigen tests, a protein called nucleoprotein (NP) is mainly the target of detection. For type A and type B, by using antibodies corresponding to each virus, it is possible to determine which type of antigen has been detected. Therefore, the test results are displayed as "Type A positive" or "Type B positive". However, there is something you should know here. Even if it is type A positive, it is usually not known whether it is H1N1 or H3N2 Even if it is determined to be "Type A positive" in a general rapid antigen test, that alone does not tell you whether it is H1N1 or H3N2. Similarly, even if it is known to be "Type B positive," standard rapid antigen tests do not distinguish the lineage of type B. To investigate more detailed classifications, genetic testing or similar methods tailored to the purpose are required. Some nucleic acid amplification tests, such as PCR, can determine not only type A or B but also subtypes of type A, such as H1N1 or H3N2. However, not all PCR tests can identify the subtype. The information obtained depends on which genetic region is being tested. Knowing that a test result is "Influenza A" is different from knowing "which subtype of A it is." Is there a difference in detection sensitivity between A and B? There is one more thing you should know when looking at test results. It has been reported that rapid antigen tests tend to have lower detection sensitivity for type B compared to type A. The US CDC also cites this point as a limitation of rapid antigen tests. However, actual detection performance varies depending on the product used and the conditions under which the specimen was collected. It is not necessarily the case that all test kits have the same difference. Also, for both type A and type B, a negative rapid antigen test does not completely rule out infection. Test results must be judged in conjunction with symptoms, the surrounding epidemic situation, and clinical findings. 5. Can I catch type B after having type A? Since type A and type B are different viruses, being infected with type A does not completely prevent infection with type B. Therefore, it is possible to catch both type A and type B in the same epidemic season. Also, even with the same type A, if the subtype or the nature of the virus is different, the immunity gained from previous infections may not work sufficiently. However, just because you have a fever again after having the flu does not necessarily mean you have been infected with a different type. Since other infectious diseases or complications are also possible, it is important to consult a medical institution if symptoms persist or if they improve once and then worsen. 6. Does the vaccine cover both type A and type B? Influenza vaccines are made with both type A and type B in mind. The following three types have been selected for the manufacturing strains of the influenza HA vaccine to be used in Japan for the 2026/27 season. Domestic influenza HA vaccine production strains for the 2026/27 season Type/Subtype/Lineage selected production strains A (H1N1) pdm09 A/Switzerland/6849/2025 A (H3N2) A/Michigan/105/2025 B-type Victoria lineage B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 A combination of three types in total, two A-type strains and one B-type strain, is called a "trivalent vaccine." The "production strains" referred to here are the virus strains used to manufacture the vaccine. Inactivated HA vaccines used in Japan utilize antigens derived from production strains, and do not contain infectious viruses as they are. Previously, quadrivalent vaccines targeting both the Victoria and Yamagata lineages of B-type were also used. However, since no confirmed detections of naturally circulating B-type Yamagata lineage viruses have been reported since March 2020, the composition of the vaccine has been reviewed. However, receiving the vaccine does not completely prevent infection or the onset of Influenza A or B. The effectiveness of the vaccine also varies depending on differences in antigenicity from the viruses circulating that year, as well as the age and immune status of the person vaccinated. Nevertheless, it is one of the important measures for preventing the onset and severity of influenza. Also, the necessity of treatment is not determined solely by the difference between A-type and B-type. Treatment is determined by considering the severity of symptoms, risk of becoming severe, and the time elapsed since onset. 7. Summary Influenza A and B are both viruses that cause seasonal influenza, but their classification mechanisms differ. A-type is divided into subtypes such as H1N1 and H3N2, while B-type has classifications known as the Victoria and Yamagata lineages. On the other hand, because both cause similar symptoms, it is not possible to determine the type based on symptoms alone. Also, while general rapid antigen tests can distinguish between A-type and B-type, they cannot identify the A-type subtype or B-type lineage. What we would like to convey from the laboratory is that there are things that can and cannot be understood from "Type A positive" or "Type B positive" results. By knowing the meaning of the terms written in the test results, perhaps your understanding of influenza will deepen. Seasonal influenza activity continues to rise across much of the US and is higher than normally seen at this time of year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) latest weekly surveillance report. Clinical laboratories reported 9.1% of respiratory specimens testing positive for influenza during the week ending Oct 31. Clinical laboratories tested 51,351 specimens that week, and 4,696 were positive. Cumulative positivity since Oct 4 stands at 6.8% of 233,110 specimens tested. Influenza A accounted for 98.6% of positive clinical lab specimens. Positivity rose nationally and in most regions. It held stable in region 7 and fell in region 9, which CDC says could reflect incomplete reporting. CDC cautioned that an earlier rise in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak or greater overall severity. All data are preliminary. H1N1 Predominates in Public Health Lab Data Of the 513 influenza-positive specimens reported by public health laboratories, 502 were influenza A and 11 were influenza B. Among the 388 influenza A viruses that were subtyped, 379 (97.7%) were A(H1N1)pdm09, 7 (1.8%) were A(H3N2), and 2 (0.5%) were A(H5). Since late May, 83.4% of reported influenza A viruses have been A(H1N1)pdm09, most of them in the D.3.1.1 HA subclade. CDC noted that recently circulating D.3.1.1 viruses have split into distinct groups with different genetic changes in their HA genes, and the agency is seeing more genetic diversity among co-circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses than before. The agency said it is too early to know which viruses will predominate or whether there are implications for vaccine effectiveness this season. Among the 688 influenza viruses CDC has genetically characterized since May 24, 486 were A(H1N1)pdm09, 106 were A(H3N2), and 96 were B/Victoria. Of the A(H3N2) viruses, 101 (95.3%) belonged to subclade K. Related: FDA Clears Roche Respiratory Panel with Expanded Pathogen Coverage Vaccine Match and Antiviral Susceptibility CDC’s antigenic testing found most characterized viruses are well recognized by antisera raised against the 2026-2027 Northern Hemisphere vaccine reference viruses: A(H1N1)pdm09: 140 of 147 viruses (95.2%) were well recognized by antisera to the A/Missouri/11/2025-like reference virus. A(H3N2): all 35 viruses were well recognized by antisera to the A/Darwin/1415/2025-like reference virus. B/Victoria: all 33 viruses were well recognized by antisera to the B/Pennsylvania/14/2025-like reference virus. On antiviral susceptibility, 8 of 654 viruses tested (1.2%) showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. All were A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses carrying the NA-I223V and NA-S247N substitutions. No viruses showed reduced inhibition by peramivir or zanamivir, and none showed decreased susceptibility to baloxavir. Related: Blood Test Predicts How Long Vaccine Immunity Will Last Two New H5 Infections in Washington CDC reported two confirmed human infections with avian influenza A(H5) virus, including one death. The Washington State Department of Health reported both cases in adults who worked at commercial dairy cattle farms where highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has been detected in cows. The first patient developed respiratory symptoms during the week ending October 24, went to an emergency department the following week, was hospitalized, and died. The testing pathway involved several laboratories. A specimen collected at the health care facility was presumptive positive for influenza A(H5) at the University of Washington, then confirmed at the Washington State Public Health Laboratory using the CDC influenza A(H5) assay. Additional testing by the University of Washington identified the virus as A(H5N1). The second patient developed conjunctivitis, and the state public health laboratory confirmed influenza A(H5) during the week ending October 31. The specimen has been shipped to CDC for additional testing. Washington has now reported three influenza A(H5) cases in dairy workers. Human-to-human transmission of avian influenza A(H5) has not been identified in the US. Related: Diagnostic Testing Is First Line of Defense Against H5N1 Related: Labcorp Launches H5 Bird Flu Test Hospitalizations, Outpatient Visits, and Deaths Severe disease indicators are also trending upward. Hospitals reported 8,396 patients admitted with laboratory-confirmed influenza during the week, a rate of 2.5 per 100,000 population. The cumulative hospitalization rate in FluSurv-NET is 6.0 per 100,000. The highest rate is among adults 65 and older, at 19.8 per 100,000. Among hospitalized patients with subtype information, 99.2% had A(H1N1)pdm09. Outpatient and emergency department measures are rising as well: 2.8% of outpatient visits were for influenza-like illness, up from the previous week but still below the national baseline of 2.9%. 1.7% of emergency department visits carried an influenza discharge diagnosis, also an increase. Two jurisdictions reported high influenza-like illness activity, and five reported moderate activity. Influenza accounted for 0.3% of deaths during the week, a figure that has remained stable week to week but has trended upward over the past 7 weeks. Two pediatric deaths from the 2026-2027 season were reported this week, bringing the season total to three. Three additional deaths from the 2025-2026 season were also reported, bringing that season’s total to 202. CDC’s preliminary in-season assessment classifies severity as low across all age groups, though it may change as activity increases. The agency estimates at least 1.7 million illnesses, 25,000 hospitalizations, and 1,400 deaths so far this season. Related: FDA Clears Sekisui Diagnostics Rapid COVID-19 and Flu A&B Combo Test Forecast and Recommendations CDC’s FluSight forecasts predict a likely national increase in both flu hospital admissions and the percentage of emergency department visits due to flu for the week ending November 21. New admissions are projected to range from 6,900 to 30,100, and emergency department visits from 1.6% to 6.7%. CDC continues to recommend annual influenza vaccination for people 6 months and older, and urges those not yet vaccinated this season to get vaccinated now. The agency also notes that prescription antivirals should be started as early as possible, particularly for patients at higher risk for complications. Is a Mutated H1N1 Strain to Blame? Flu activity is surging earlier than usual as an influenza A H1N1 strain with a new mutation spreads across the U.S. Here’s what to know. Updated Nov. 6, 2026, 12:57 PM EST / Source: TODAY Caroline Kee Health reporter Flu Season Kicks off Early: Is it Too Late to Get the Vaccine? 03:20 Share Add TODAY to Google If you’re surprised to hear about people getting the flu in October, you’re not alone. The 2026-2027 flu season got off to an early and strong start in the United States, experts say. Influenza activity is still considered low nationally, but cases are rising quickly in many parts of the country, especially in the West. As of Nov. 5, flu infections are growing or likely growing in 42 states, according to the latest estimates from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That’s not unusual, given that flu activity typically ramps up around this time of year. However, this year’s flu season started way ahead of schedule, with infections rising as early as August. “Early-season influenza activity is currently higher than typically observed at this time of year,” the CDC said in its FluView surveillance report for the week ending Oct. 31. So far this season, there have been at least 1,700,000 illnesses, 25,000 hospitalizations and 1,400 deaths from the flu in the U.S., per the CDC. H1N1, a type of influenza A virus, is currently fueling the vast majority of cases. That’s a shift from last winter, when influenza A H3N2 subclade K (aka, the “superflu”) was the dominant strain nationwide. What’s more, it appears that the H1N1 strain circulating in the U.S. has picked up a new mutation which may affect its ability to evade pre-existing immunity, experts say. If H1N1 sounds familiar, that’s because it’s the infamous “swine flu” virus that caused a pandemic in 2009. As the mutated H1N1 strain spreads, doctors are urging people to get the 2026-2027 flu vaccine. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu season and how to protect yourself. Why Is Flu Season Starting So Early? No two flu seasons look the same because the timing and severity can vary from year to year. It’s still too early to tell if this flu season will end up being more severe or what role the mutated H1N1 strain might play, the CDC tells TODAY.com in a statement. However, there are multiple indicators that flu activity is already higher than usual for this time of year. Cases started increasing in late August and early September and have been rising steadily since, per the CDC. The percent of flu tests coming back positive was 9.1% during the week ending Oct. 31. Last year during the same time period, the weekly test positivity rate was less than 1%, per the CDC National Respiratory and Enteric Virus Surveillance System dashboard. Outpatient visits to healthcare providers for flu-like illness hit 2.8% during the week ending Oct. 17, which is higher than the previous two seasons, CDC data show. Hospitalizations and deaths from the flu are also rising. “Cases are still relatively low, so we’re still in the early phases of a flu surge,” Andrew Pekosz, Ph.D., a virologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. As of Oct. 31, seven states are reporting moderate to high levels of flu activity: California, Florida, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Texas and Washington. It’s unclear why exactly cases are rising earlier than normal. One potential reason is that people may have less pre-existing immunity to the H1N1 strain with a new mutation. “Maybe that’s why people are getting sick sooner,” Dr. Bernard Camins, an infectious disease physician and professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, tells TODAY.com. The H1N1 strain spreading is different from the H3N2 strain that dominated last winter. “Even people who got the flu last year are vulnerable,” says Camins. When H1N1 started ramping up in late August, the updated flu shots had just started rolling out. “The pattern we oftentimes see with early season flu is that the first strain that gets here is the one that escapes immunity the most,” Pekosz adds. Does an early flu season mean a more severe flu season? Not necessarily, experts say. “An earlier increase in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak,” the CDC said in its latest FluView report. It’s too early to tell how the 2026-2027 flu season will pan out, or whether it’ll be milder compared to last year’s season. The U.S. saw a harsh flu season last winter fueled by the highly mutated H3N2 subclade K variant, aka the “super flu.” “We still have to see how bad it will be this year, but I think it is just starting earlier,” says Camins. “The only thing predictable about the flu is that it’s unpredictable,” Dr. Natalie Azar, NBC News medical contributor, said on TODAY. What Is the Mutated H1N1 Strain? Influenza viruses mutate constantly, which is why we get an updated flu shot every year. Last summer, flu A H3N2 picked up a host of mutations, which led to the emergence the subclade K variant. H1N1 viruses typically change less often than H3N2 viruses, the CDC says. However, this year, H1N1 (pdm09), subclade D.3.1.1, acquired one new mutation, G155E, says Pekosz. The mutation was first identified in September in Seattle, Washington, according in a preprint paper published to bioRxiv. “It is different from last year’s H1N1 virus, and that mutation position (G155E) we know is important for generating protective antibody responses,” Pekosz explains. This means the latest H1N1 strain may be better able to escape immunity because the antibodies people have from previous infection or vaccination may not recognize it as well. “How that (mutation) is going to affect the disease spread and severity is not clear,” says Pekosz. Even if the H1N1 strain circulating does not match the one included in the 2026-2027 flu vaccines, the shot is still expected to provide protection. “A mismatch is not a black-or-white situation. We may have less immunity, not no immunity,” Pekosz adds. Historically, H1N1 has hit young people particularly hard. The new mutation may make children more susceptible, especially if they haven’t been exposed to H1N1 yet, Azar said. “It is too early to know what viruses may predominate or to say whether there might be implications on flu vaccine effectiveness this season,” the CDC said in its latest FluView report. H1N1 Flu Symptoms Influenza often hits suddenly and intensely, says Camins. Common symptoms of the flu include: Fever Chills Fatigue Body aches Runny nose Coughing It can be difficult to distinguish the signs of a flu infection from those caused by COVID-19, which is why testing is important, Camins says. If you test positive for influenza, you can seek treatment with antivirals, which can lessen symptom severity and duration. Antivirals are an especially important tool for high-risk groups, including people over the age of 65, children under the age of 5, and immunocompromised individuals. These medications aren’t available over-the-counter, so you’ll need to see a doctor first. “You have to get that prescription fast ... within the first 48 hours after symptom onset, (or else) they don’t work as well,” says Pekosz. If you experience severe flu symptoms, contact your doctor. When to Get the Flu Shot There’s no reason to panic over the mutated H1N1 strain, the experts emphasize, but it is a good reminder to protect yourself. “View (this) as a a sign to go out and get the flu vaccine,” says Pekosz. Getting a flu shot is the most effective way to prevent against severe illness, complications and death from the flu. The 2026-2027 flu vaccines are available at most pharmacies, doctors’ offices and clinics. The updated shots protect against three viruses: influenza A H1N1 (pdm09), influenza A H3N2 and influenza B. There are multiple options available, including standard flu shots, high-dose shots, a nasal mist and the new mRNA flu vaccine. “Even if there’s a mismatched strain, there’s two other strains that the vaccine will provide better protection against,” says Pekosz. Different flu strains can circulate later in the season, so the shot can protect you throughout the winter and early spring. The flu shot is never 100% effective, Camins adds, and you can still get infected if you’ve been vaccinated — but you won’t get nearly as sick or end up in the hospital. Vaccination is especially important if you’re considered high-risk, but everyone can benefit. The best time to get the flu shot is before the end of October, but the vaccine will still provide protection if you get it later in the season, the experts note. “If you haven’t gotten it yet for whatever reason, now’s the time to get vaccinated because the flu season is starting a little bit sooner and you need at least two weeks for the vaccine immunity to (reach) protective levels,” Pekosz adds. If you aren’t sure which flu vaccine you should get, talk to your doctor or pharmacist. Share Add TODAY to Google Caroline Kee Caroline Kee is a health reporter at TODAY based in New York City. She covers a range of medical news, consumer health, and wellness topics. supplementary_news.content_title: 流感盯上孩子!家长如何科学认识和有效预防?_腾讯新闻
supplementary_news.content: 流感盯上孩子!家长如何科学认识和有效预防? 陇原健康 2026-11-06 20:03发布于甘肃陇原健康官方账号 问AI · 流感疫苗每年更新配方基于何种流行趋势? 每年秋冬季节,儿童流感都会成为家长们关心的焦点。根据国家流感中心最新监测[1],北方阳性率略有上升,南方略有下降。全国流感阳性样本中,甲型占67.6%、乙型占32.4%;甲型中以H3N2为主,H1N1也占一定比例,乙型均为B(Victoria)系。可见甲型H3N2、甲型H1N1和乙型B(Victoria)系流感病毒都在传播,并不是某一种病毒“一家独大” ,且目前监测的流感病毒对常用的两类抗流感药物总体仍保持敏感。家长不用费劲猜到底是哪一种,更重要的是观察孩子症状和精神状态,必要时及时就医。 儿童流感的症状特点 流感通常起病较急,发热、乏力、头痛、肌肉酸痛等全身症状往往比普通感冒更明显。不管是H3N2、H1N1还是乙型流感,孩子都可能出现:发烧、咳嗽、嗓子疼、头疼、浑身没劲、肌肉酸痛等症状。有些孩子感染乙型流感后,还可能出现恶心、呕吐、拉肚子的症状。但要提醒一句:不能因为孩子吐了,就认定是乙流,也不能因为烧得高,就认定是甲流。 该图片疑似使用了AI生成技术,请谨慎甄别 01 0~3岁儿童: 流感的症状不典型,可能表现出食欲不振、呕吐、腹泻、易哭闹、呼吸急促等症状。新生儿可能仅表现为嗜睡、拒奶、呼吸暂停,需要家长格外留意。 02 3~6岁儿童: 多表现为明显的发热、咳嗽和喉咙痛,活动较平时有减少,进入公共场所,与他人保持安全社交距离,勤洗手,戴好口罩。 03 6岁以上儿童: 症状接近成人,可能出现寒战、高热,全身症状(肌肉酸痛、乏力等)较明显。 特别提醒: 如果孩子本身还有哮喘、心脏病、神经系统疾病或免疫功能较弱,更要早点看医生。 怀疑流感,必要时还是要“验一验” 流感季里,孩子突然发烧、浑身没劲、肌肉酸痛,确实要想到流感。但秋冬季呼吸道病毒很多,流感、呼吸道合胞病毒、腺病毒等,有时症状很相似。所以,如果孩子年龄小、症状重、有基础疾病,或者病情越来越重,应及时就医,由医生判断是否需要进行流感抗原、核酸等检查。 需要提醒的是,抗原检测阴性也不能百分之百排除流感。 该图片疑似使用了AI生成技术,请谨慎甄别 何时需要立即就医? 需要提醒家长的是,若儿童出现发热、咳嗽、咽痛等流感症状,同时还有以下情况: 01 精神和神志改变,如反应迟钝、嗜睡、烦躁、惊厥 02 呼吸困难和/或呼吸频率加快 03 严重呕吐、腹泻,出现脱水表现 04 尿量明显减少,四肢末梢冰冷,皮肤颜色差 05 原有基础疾病(如哮喘)明显加重 06 高热持续不退、喂养困难等 治疗抓住“黄金48小时” 记住“1个黄金时间(48小时内)、2类手段(抗病毒药+护理)、3个禁忌(不滥用抗生素、不硬扛、不混搭药)”,就能科学应对流感,守护自己和家人健康! 1 症状出现48小时内是抗病毒治疗的“黄金窗口期”,但不是治疗“截止线”。对于病情较重、持续加重或属于高风险人群的孩子,即使超过48小时,也应及时就医,由医生评估是否需要抗病毒治疗。 2 尽早就医确诊,进行病原学检测 3 遵医嘱使用抗病毒药物,切勿自行用药 4 不滥用抗生素(对病毒无效) 5 不混合使用多种药物 轻症患儿居家护理要点 对于轻症流感患儿可居家隔离,居家期间应当密切关注体温变化,观察咳嗽、咳痰、呼吸困难等症状是否加重,遵医嘱用药。同时还应做到: 保证充足的睡眠,避免劳累; 多喝水,均衡饮食,摄入富含蛋白质、维生素和矿物质的食物; 注意个人卫生,勤洗手,房间保持通风,定时清洁地面; 患儿咳嗽时应用干净的手绢、纸巾或衣袖遮盖口鼻,及时清理污染物; 家庭成员应尽量保持距离、戴口罩,注意防护。 预防是关键 1.疫苗接种 每年的流感病毒都会有些变化,流感疫苗也会根据流行情况进行调整。每年接种流感疫苗是预防流感、降低重症和并发症风险的重要措施。建议在9—10月尽早完成接种,如果错过了这个时间,在整个流感流行季仍然可以接种。 2.养成良好卫生习惯 勤洗手 保持环境清洁和通风 在流感流行季尽量避免去人群聚集场所,避免接触呼吸道感染患者 咳嗽或打喷嚏时,用上臂或纸巾、毛巾等遮住口鼻,随后及时洗手,避免接触眼睛、鼻或口 家庭成员出现流感患者时要尽量避免互相接触,出现流感症状的患儿去医院就诊时,应做好防护(如戴口罩),避免交叉感染 返校提醒 流感患儿平均排毒时间为4~8天,即使在症状出现48小时内接受抗流感病毒治疗,患儿的平均排毒时间仍为3~5天。中位退热时间为2天,这意味着即使孩子退热、流感症状好转,后续仍可能持续排毒约2天。 因此,建议流感患儿体温恢复正常、症状消失48小时后再返校,降低流感校园传播风险。 流感虽然凶猛,但科学应对可有效预防。愿每个孩子都能呼吸顺畅,健康成长,拥抱每一个清新的冬日。 参考文献: [1]中国疾病预防控制中心。2026年第43周第932期中国流感监测周报[EB/OL].2026-10-28.中国疾控中心第43周流感监测周报。 [2]中国疾病预防控制中心.中国流感疫苗预防接种技术指南(2026—2027)[EB/OL].(2026-09-02)[2026-11-05].中国流感疫苗预防接种技术指南(2026—2027) (来源:兰州大学第一医院) 主办丨甘肃省卫生健康委 编辑制作丨新甘肃·每日甘肃网、省卫生健康宣教中心 审核丨一审 庞传伟、常晓婷 审核丨二审 安 娜、马 菁、白 雪 审核丨三审 杨敬科、陆一鸣
